utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al [Realtime transcript read in error, "Momcilo Perisic"]. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, 13th of January, 2009. I said 2009 because it seems that it is 2008 on the transcript still, so we really have to keep a tight watch on everything in this courtroom. I'll first greet the witness. Good afternoon to the accused, the Defence counsel, Mr. Stringer and all the Prosecution team, and good afternoon to all the people assisting us. We are going to continue with this witness's testimony. You may proceed, Mr. Karnavas. Again, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cvikl.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand it, we left off yesterday with slide 27. That's when I cut you off a little bit because we were out of time, and so now we are getting into slide 28, so without further adieu, if you could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Karnavas. We now have a new court reporter, and I see another mistake on line 6 on page 1. This is Prlic et al and not Momcilo Perisic as you can see on line 6. I'm not going to spend my time on spotting mistakes, but if anyone does, they should tell me so that I could take a rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Well, at some point we do know that the transcript will be cleaned up, and we know that these sorts of errors do occur rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Cvikl, if we can now turn to slide 28 so we can complete this section before we go on to the three phases, and you can begin.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, Mr. Karnavas. I would like to make just one observation before we start. Last night, I went through my testimony and I also the check of the report and especially of the documents which have been listed under the previous slide, the slide 27, and I would like just to confirm for the record that what I have seen for the first time were English translations of those documents. However, I've seen the original, the Croatian versions or the Bosnian version of those documents before, but as we were preparing over the weekends for the first time I have seen the English translation. That's all that need to be said with this. In regards to the slide 28. In this slide 28, I tried to summarise what is actually one of my findings on activities of local communities, and that is I have been asked to compare those activities, and as we have seen yesterday when you were presenting many documents on four major group of measures, measures to ensure defence, macroeconomic measures, microeconomic measures, and measures to ensure government services. Notwithstanding whether these were measures undertaken in the local community with -- under the Bosnian control or with a Croat majority, I have not been seeing what was happening in Republika Srpska. But these were practically equal measures and those really equal measures in practically all major areas. They were all based on the task of the local communities as defined in the old constitution both of Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were actually measures by local communities to ensure logistic and the finance of defence, and then there were measures were in the absence of the actions of the state authorities, the central government authorities, they were undertaking macroeconomic measures or they were undertaking measures to support and to provide state and social services to the citizens. That's why I say that situation in Tuzla, Jablanica, Maglaj, Mostar, Livno, Travnik, Zenica, Siroki Brijeg, Posusje, they were measures were all equal. Logically why these local communities have to do that, since there was a practically complete loss of communications and they were cut off from the republic level provision of funds for those services, they had to ensure economic stability in the economic area that they controlled, and they had to provide -- ensure fiscal revenues to provide social services, and I mentioned some of them in the bracket in the second bullet. So to certain extent, local communities acted like sovereign economies with a task to cover the basic needs of the citizens, to provide material support to the defence forces, and, of course, that was the basis, normalization of the life conditions for the people; once the defence was assured, that was the basis for reactivation of economic activities. I'm also saying in the report and would like to reiterate here that these were urgent actions by local authorities and they were actually done in the circumstances of war economy, and in that context they acted as one would act in similar conditions, notwithstanding what kind of the political intentions were behind. But I was looking into the measures, and I can confirm these were the measures done in the interest of all citizens in different local communities throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Unless there are any questions regarding this area, we can now move on to slide 29, and hereinafter, as I understand your presentation following your report, you describe what you came up with, the three different phases of the Croatian community, Croatian Republic, Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I have been, of course, asked to analyse, and in order to somehow identify differences in the -- in the situation in the Croatian -- in the Croatian community of the Herceg-Bosna, I actually divided this into three areas. The first area -- the first period or the first phase is really the phase when we have activities only at the level of the local communities, and some limited activity by the presidency of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna; the second phase is then the phase when the executive authority had been established, the HVO of the Croatian community of the Herceg-Bosna; and the third phase and last one is the one when the parliament had been established and when the executive authority had been renamed itself in government and where they continue with the region-wide measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Cvikl. Now, if we look on slide 29, there are some bullet points, and as I understand that you wanted to draw our attention to certain documents. So if we could begin, that is, if you could give us a -- some remarks before we go into each particular bullet.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to bring me my documents because they stayed here. Okay. What was done in the first phase, what was done in the first phase at the level of the local community of -- local communities of Herceg-Bosna, there was, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. Sorry for interrupting you. Let me go back to what you said earlier on, which was absolutely essential and extremely relevant for the further deliberations of judges as to the joint criminal enterprise. If I understand you properly, you said that we must grasp a situation at three levels: First level, that is the creation by local communities of some action plan in this field; second level, the Croatian community or HVO has been created; third stage, as you say, that would be somehow a parliamentary phase because then the parliament has been established, which is to control the executive authority. And you seem to break down all of the events based on the three levels, and that could account for a great number of things. The local level, that's the first level of intervention; second level, that's HVO; the third one being parliamentary control. Is that what you meant? I just want to ask you this for everything to be clear for everyone because this is a very intricate issue, and it really is worthy of comprehensive examination and scrutiny without avoiding any misunderstanding to start with. Can you indeed confirm that as far as you see, the measures undertaken have to be seen from the point of view of these three levels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What am I writing in the report is that there were three phases of development, not three levels, one above the other, but three phases, one after another. Why three phases? My report, and I was asked to do -- to analyse the economic measures and development in the area -- in the Croatian community, Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna within the context of what was happening in the overall Bosnia-Herzegovina. As we were explaining what was happening first at the local community level, I have also seen that in the similar manner as in Tuzla region, the local communities that compound the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna acted in a very similar manner in that first very phase. Once they were acting as explained in this light, which means that they organised the defence, they organised economic sector, they, of course, ensure protection of the state -- yeah, the state regional assets, they collected new fiscal revenues, they allocated fiscal revenues into budget. Then there was immediate negative results of them acting independently because each of them acted in their own territory of a local community or municipality. So in the second phase of the developments, in order to assure region-wide measures, in order to ensure that, also, those local communities that were not -- maybe not backed so well off as some of them would also benefit from the region-wide measures. I'll give an example. The local communities at which there was physically a checking cross-point of goods coming from Republic of Croatia into Bosnia-Herzegovina, they benefitted because they were collecting customs. We've seen some of the measures yesterday undertaken in Capljina. So now in the second phase, the executive -- the authority, the HVO of the Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna has been established, and it had to assure that not all funds stay in just one local community because there were needs in other local community, you know, to undertake government, social, and state services. So in this second phase, HVO acted to ensure that there will be -- we call economist economy of scale or we say that there will be economic region-wide measures so that the balance of the economic development and the benefit of economic development would be provided to the whole region of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And so that is then the second phase, and I've seen that there is a difference between the first phase when you have only actions by the local communities, and there's a different with the second phase where you have, you know, executive authority, HVO, undertaking some measures and actually fighting, "economically fighting," with local communities to take part of that -- some assets collected locally into the region-wide budget. And the third phase, time-wise, is the phase when this executive authority have been strengthened because the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna had been established, and as we have seen, especially the second half of 1993 and early 1994, then you have government of these Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna acting, again, with economic measures, like established budget, and, of course, undertaking some of the measures. And I'm also saying, and we will see this down the slides, that the reason why in the second phase and in the third phase authorities, regional authorities appeared is also connected with the realisation by the presidency of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which already in August 1992 realised that unless local communities are grouped in what they call districts or counties, the country would economically collapse. So in the second and in the third phase, the activity which I have seen in the Croatian Community and later Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna are actually activity vested into them both by the constitution and by a decree of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the work of the districts, and that is what I then also comment in my document in one of the slides later that had been done. But, yes, there are three phases down the line, one after another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I can understand what you say by the three phases based on economic reasoning, but if in my mind, and possibly in any reasonable mind, there's always a connection with a political factor because economics and politics, that's a couple; that's a pair. This reasoning that you've just set forth in economic terms, can it be applied to the political sphere, so there would have been three phases in political terms. There would have been power vested with the local communities, thereafter a second phase in which the Croatian community was created with, as a third phase, the creation of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. So if you put together, if you link up the political and the economics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have been asked to analyse economic measures. And so in that context, I cannot comment on the political intentions. But, you know, I'm politician, and of course when I act either as the minister or when I acted as a general secretary, we are working under a particular programme; and the programme, if you want a political programme in this very area, was ensure the survival of the population. And in that context, the political decisions both at the level of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as at the level of the Presidency of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina have the same aim, ensure the survival of the population, because otherwise -- I was surprised to a certain extent but positively surprised seeing this presidency decree on districts or on counties because it actually politically realised that if central government is landlocked in Sarajevo, in order for the population to survive, but not survive in 50 or 70, you know, small local economies controlled by municipality, people would be better off if there would be seven districts, seven counties established, and there would be rounding of economic measures at the wider region. This is how I see this second and third phase. The second and third phase of development in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was to round economic -- economic area to further support economic developments and thus ensure not just the survival of the people, because the military activities more or less were over, but to ensure better economic conditions. And if I go one more step, even later when the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established following the Washington Agreement - there's a time when the war loan was start coming in - we have seen a lot of legislation, which was simply if you want legislation of then-Croatian Community or Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna transmitted to the level of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So even when one analyse those economic measures, these were measures for the benefit of ensuring -- to the ensure the economic benefits to the people in the wider region, not just the very small local community. And that's why I'm saying, yes, there is a link between the economics and the politics, but the economics and the economic needs of the population were out there. If I may, maybe for these people would be, you know, maybe even better not to deal with these all issues. They would simply let, you know, borders not being established and this would slowly economically -- this part would be slowly economically completely integrated with Dalmatia, which is, as we all know, part of the Republic of Croatia. Now, there were attempts to round economic economies of the local communities in this Croatian Community of the Herceg-Bosna into an area that later merged into the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could stay -- staying with slide 29, and if we -- we did discuss briefly the various bullet points, and we can start with the first one, to organise the wartime finances, and as I understand you wanted to draw our attention as a way of example to 1D 00558.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. This is the document issued by the Croatian Defence Council of the Mostar municipality, an action of the local community of Mostar to organise, establish a decision on the organisation and functioning of wartime finances. And in Roman ii, in Article 3, it says: "The following financial organisation shall continue to operate in war." And here, the public auditing service or the Social Accounting Office is mentioned, the Privredna Banka Sarajevo with its basic bank in Mostar. And in Article 4, it says that some of the institution shall cease to operate because they did not have conditions, but what is important, it says in Article 10, that revenues generated from profit tax shall be deposited in a separate account of the municipality. And then in Roman iii, Article 11, there was also a proposition that the Mostar municipality HVO may float a war loan on the basis of voluntary subscription. And on Roman iv, on page -- on the bottom, 1D25-0158, in Articles 14, 15, et cetera, the financing of public services is described. So this very decision of the Mostar municipality describes what the local community of Mostar will undertake to provide, not just for the defence but to cover basic needs of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go on to the next bullet point, to organise economic sector, I understand there are three documents you want to draw our attention to, the first one being 1D 00239.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- just as an example of a very similar decision. This is a decision of Tuzla municipal assembly to proclaim enterprises and financial institutions of special importance for Tuzla municipality in conditions of war. And here it says in Article 1, Roman ii, point 1, the term of power system, Kreka, socially owned enterprise, Tuzla, is a company which is of a special importance for Tuzla municipality in conditions of war. And in -- on the next page in Roman vii, it says under 1, that Tuzla public auditing service is such an institution, and that -- in point 2, that commercial banks Tuzlanska banka did it, Tuzla comerciana [phoen] banka did it, Tuzla Union banka did it. Sarajevo, Tuzla branch are companies, institutions important for a situation in Tuzla, just an example how in a similar manner as in Mostar, also in Tuzla regions, same type of institutions were recognised as important to organise economic sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go on to the next document concerning this particular bullet point, and I believe it's 1D 02991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that is a decision by Prozor municipality. It's a decision on announcement of general mobilisation in the area of Prozor municipality, but it's even more. In Article 2, it says that: "All persons, men of the age 18 to 55 years and woman of the age 18 to 50, with residence in the area of Prozor municipality are obliged to immediately be at disposal of Prozor municipality in order to be deployed to the military forces." That is, certain duties in civil protection or requisitioning of workers. So there were military forces, but there were also logistical activities of economic sector to support those forces. And second, what is important in this article -- in this decision is at the end of the -- Article 3, that workers employed abroad are obliged to make a payment in the amount of one-quarter of their salary, that is, at least 500 Deutschemark, if they are up to the period that they would, of course, respond to the announcement of general mobilisation, meaning that, again, a measure which is, yes, a wartime finances and organisation of economic sector measure undertaken in the local community in a very similar measure that we have seen in some other areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then, finally, if we go to 1D 00805, I believe this is the last document for this bullet point you wanted by way of example to explain to us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decision of Croatian Defence Council, Livno, wherein -- on first page, on the Roman i, in the first paragraph, it says that: "Mobilisation and demobilization of assets..." and in the bracket, "(vehicles, machinery, equipment, et cetera) shall be carried out by the Defence office in accordance with establishment requirements of the command of the HVO." In the second paragraph, there is a request that: "In order to effect more rational distribution and use of assets, the HVO command of the units must coordinate and redistribute assets with the Defence office." The Defence office being the one providing Defence support. And then, second what I would like to point is if you turn to page 2, that is the page marked in the bottom right 1D 15-0196, and then in Roman iii it says that work organisations whose scope of operations becomes considerably reduced as a result of mobilisation of their resources shall prepare a business plan for operating with the available assets and manpower, which means that the local community authorities through its Defence council, through its HVO clearly undertake a manage to re-organise the economic sector in the war circumstances when before a lot of assets had been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go on to the next bullet point where you talk about to ensure protection of state/regional assets. As I understand it, by way of example you wanted to draw our attention to 1D 00579. 1D 00579.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document issued on May 21st, 1992, by the Mostar municipality: "A decision on the establishment and tasks of the Mostar municipal HVO commissioners and setting up managing functions in the socially owned companies and institutions in the Mostar municipality under wartime conditions." Why this decision is important. Local municipality, in order to protect state regional assets that was vested in the local community by the - at that time - Croatia -- Yugoslav, Slovene, Croatian, Bosnian constitutions as we have seen yesterday, in Article 2 established a new function: "A commissioner of the Mostar municipal HVO who is an authorised person appointed by the Mostar municipal at the proposal of the head of the department whose task is to review the organisation of the sphere for which the commissioner is appointed..." et cetera. What is important in Article 5 on the bottom of this, it is clearly says that the Mostar municipal HVO commissioner shall be appointed for the following spheres: elementary education, secondary education, culture, traffic, telecommunication and information, non-ferrous metals industry, metal industry - next page - agriculture and food processing industry, et cetera. Even later, we have the hotel management and tourism. These are all measures that provide two things. First, assets, that I'm still socially owned assets, but of course for which the local community had an authority to protect them, were taken care of now by this commissioners, and these commissioners were not just taking care of those assets, but they were ensuring, especially in these spheres as mentioned here that are the spheres of ensuring government, social and state services, to undertake those and that especially here, education, culture, et cetera. And then, of course, they were also responsible to take care what is happening in the industry manufacturing, so a clear activity to ensure protection of state and regional assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we go on to the next bullet point where you note measures to establish and collect fiscal revenues, you wanted to draw our attention to several documents, the first being 1D 00635.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would be grateful if the witness could read slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that. Thank you for the warning. First, I would like to, of course, emphasize that this bullet reads to establish and collect new fiscal revenues, new fiscal revenues that were not in establishment before, and the first document is Document 1D 00635, a decision of the Mostar municipality of June 5th, 1992, on the war tax for workers from Mostar municipality working abroad and pensioners whose pensions were earned abroad. A lot of people from abroad -- a lot of people from Mostar local municipality worked abroad, and in Article 2, it says that: "Workers from Mostar municipality employed abroad must pay 300 German marks, Deutschemark, a month to the Mostar municipality HVO as war tax." And then in Article 3: "For the pensioners who earned their pensions abroad, but have a place of residence in Mostar ..." and this money was coming from abroad into the country or it was -- it stayed on the accounts abroad, "... must pay war tax to the Mostar municipality HVO every month." And it defines that, of course, that tax shall be 15 percent of the pension for all pensions up to 800 German marks, and for pensions above 800 German marks it was set at 150 German marks. Again, a measure by which, of course, this -- this -- this -- new fiscal revenues shall be collected. Then in Article 4, it says where this and how had war tax shall be paid. Since there were no banking up and running, the Article 4 says that: "These war tax shall be paid into the Mostar municipality HVO giro account, non-residential account, at the Splitska banka, DD joint stock company Split, or in cash at the counter of the Mostar municipal HVO office for finance." Again, a measure by which new fiscal revenues and, of course, depositing of that had been undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go on to the next document, 1D 02996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just add a question to what you have just said. Do you know by which ways, how foreign payments reached the persons concerned in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, before the war, that has been done through the banking system. There were, let's say, Yugoslav banks having branches abroad, especially in Germany, and then there was deposits. Now, with this decision, Mostar pensioners could instruct the pension fund of, let's say, a particular either enterprise or German pension funds where this money shall be deposited. And since they could not -- since the banks were not up and running in -- at that very period in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the opening of the non-residential account was the only way to do it. After, and we would see later the first banks were re-established, and the first, you know, foreign transactions were undertaken, then -- you know, then it was paid via the normal international transactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, that means that these monies were paid on accounts in banks outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, these monies, as says in Article 3 -- 4, they were paid to a non-residential account of the HVO municipality in a bank outside, a very normal situation which usually happens if you have within the country a non-functioning banking system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we go on to the next document, which is 1D 02996.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decision by the Prozor municipality on war tax to be paid out the basic personal income, and in Article 2 it says that this war tax is set at 80 percent of the net personal income. Again, a new measure, not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have heard you say, and I read, 80 percent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 80 percent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: 80, four-fifths?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's right on the document, Your Honour, Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, you are an expert witness. This is quite a surprising document because we can see that taxes levied on somebody who has personal income to the tune of 80 percent. I fail to understand. Is the tax rate 80 percent of one's income, or is the individual to be taxed on 80 percent of what that individual has earned based on a specific tax rate? How is this to be read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that had to be read as follows: When somebody was employed with a company, he received 100 units as net, and the company paid as a war tax 80 units of a war tax. So his cost to the employer was 180. Employee brought home 180 was paid to the, that case, war budget. So it's not what we know as a marginal rate of 80. It's -- as it says, Article 1: "All taxes and contributions paid out of the basic personal income shall be transformed into war tax out of the basic personal income." And the way that is done is it is on top of 100 which he receives. This is the time when there were no personal income taxation. This is the way how employer had been additionally taxed for the net income paid to the employee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Cvikl, what this meant in practice? It raises the cost of labour for the employer enormously to almost double. Would that not then have as a consequence that the salary is somewhat reduced so as to remain within a viable bracket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in old Yugoslav system, that was the way that wages were taxed. So you have a net, and then on top of the net there was so-called, so-called contributions that could go up to even 80 or above percent of the -- of the net income. Now, of course, one has to be extremely careful here. In the old time, there was a situation where companies were not able to pay the contributions on a particular net income, but you should also note that these gross wages or the difference between the net and the gross, these so-called contributions on the base of the net income were the main source of the financing, the para-fiscal funds which we were discussing yesterday. So since there was a very small sales tax in old Yugoslavia, the really major source of income of the government at large, including the para-fiscal funds, were these contributions. These were contributions for the pensions; these were contributions for the health sector, for education, et cetera. So this is a kind of a normal situation. Today in Slovenia, of course, such a personal income tax is a -- top bracket is 42. But in the time of the hyperinflation, et cetera, for many reasons, including the problem with the value of the money when the money is really collected, could go up to 80 percent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But what still puzzles me is that you speak of taxes imposed on the workers, but you say the worker received a salary of 100, and he continues to receive 100 except that the employer has to deliver the double or whatever to the state, and it turns out, looks more like an employer's tax than an employee's tax.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, but you have to be extremely careful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am. I try to be. That's why I asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war, before the war, this was a contribution which, as we discussed yesterday, employer paid to the Self-Management Interest Community, to the Social Accounting Office. At the start of the war, the Social Accounting Office at the level of the whole country ceased to exist, ceased to operate. So employers was not able to pay any contributions to the, let's say, pension fund of the -- Bosnia-Herzegovina with its account in Sarajevo, but at the same time, you know, employee, if he worked, he still was receiving net wages. So since with the decree which was -- which we discussed yesterday, local communities were authorised to issue a new type of taxations. This synthetic tax, this 80 percent war tax was a way how employer continued to pay costs linked with the employer, but the employer had to pay this now to an account of the Prozor municipality because Social Accounting Office did not work out, and they could not transfer money to the -- to, let's say, accounts of the pension fund in Sarajevo. Even more, I have not seen any opening of the non-residential account of the pension fund of Sarajevo, of the whole Bosnia-Herzegovina, where these monies shall be paid. So there was an absence of a new legislation, I haven't seen it, where they would eventually say, okay, you employers in Prozor and elsewhere, give money that you would otherwise, normal circumstances, if the communication would be up and running, paying to accounts of the pension funds in Sarajevo, pay it somewhere else. So this was a logical reaction by the Prozor municipality since they have to take care of the people. They have to take care of the defence. They were not receiving funds from Sarajevo. They would -- they replaced these what used to be payments of the contributions and other -- yeah, contributions from the -- on the top of the net wages to this -- into this war tax.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm trying to be careful. That's why I -- I'm not yet quite clear. These 80 percent, if I understand you now correctly, do not really mean a new additional tax that is to be paid, but it has the effect that what was due anyway, instead of going to social funds, now goes to war effort funds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, to be clear because it does seem to me to be rather complicated. I'll take two situations. I'm a policeman at the Prozor police station in July 1992. Let's say that I'm earning 100 Croatian dinars, just 100 for the sake of clarity. How much will I pay by way of tax on that income?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are a policeman and your net wage is 100, the police station as your employer would have to pay 80 dinars to the Prozor municipality. Now, since the police function is a state function, you could have a situation where they were netting this off. So there were no real transaction because police station could only get money for paying policemans from the Prozor municipality. But if you are shop assistant in Prozor, and shop assistant makes 100, then of course an owner of the shop assistant who makes money out of selling goods would have to pay to Prozor municipality 80 dinars on top of 100 dinar of the shop assistant's net pay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That was the -- that was the second situation that I wished to put to you. You've answered. If I am a shop assistant and I earn 100, according to what you say, the owner of the shop will pay 80; I continue to earn my 100 dinars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is exactly. That time, there were no personal income taxation, which is a follow-up development, so the shop assistant would take home -- would take home --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's where there is a mystery. How come, whereas we're in a period of war where everyone must contribute to the war effort those who are not earning, those who have an income, be they policeman or shop assistant, don't personally contribute themselves to the taxes, to war taxes? Why was that not put in place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a shop assistant or -- the situation is same before the war and once the war started. He paid -- he got 100 dinars, and the owner paid 80. There were some other measures that we have seen that they did not -- they were not increasing the wages, but him working and him continuing paying -- receiving 100 wages, he was to a certain extent contributing to the war effort. So that's, I mean -- I would not -- I have not seen that now the shop assistant would receive less net wage, less net wage. He would receive the same 100, but the shop owner would continue to pay 80 - that's how it was defined here - to the Prozor municipality to provide funds for the, you know, things that Prozor had to undertake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand, because all this is rather complicated, in fact, the citizen, whether he is a policeman working in a barber shop or an employee for a company, doesn't himself contribute through the tax to the war effort; it's his employer, not him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we have discussed yesterday that most of the socially owned enterprises practically collapsed, so these were what really, you know, enable the survival of the population were, you know, really private traders, private shops. So whether this shop assistant is a son of an owner or a brother of an owner or he himself an owner, I don't know. I mean, I didn't go into the test, but I did not have a feeling that there would be, you know, a new personal income tax imposed by which he would receive less of a -- less of a net wage. I mean, he anyhow had to survive in this difficult circumstances. And I would even claim that since, you know, for any economic area you need to have people there, taxing them additionally would mean that, you know, they would pack and they would go. So I don't see from an economic point of view imposing additional person income tax by which shop assistants would take home less would be beneficial. Most likely, this Bosnian dinars or whatever he was earning, given the fact that there was a limited supply of goods, did not actually buy the same amount of kilos of bread, litres of milk, et cetera, than it was before the war. So everybody was taking, you know, a hit. In what form, it's difficult to say. I was not doing the analysis of particular households, you know, looking to what was the so-called disposable income of a particular family. But I don't see an economic instrument, the one you are suggesting, as a useful measure in wartime circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 02997.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document by the same Prozor municipality, which is a decision on a location of funds by the workers employed abroad for the needs of defence of Prozor municipality. And here, again, as in some other, those who are employed abroad in Article 1st and have a permanent residence in Prozor municipality are obliged to allocate 30 percent of their monthly net salary for the needs of the defence. And then in Article 3 says that those who do not want to allocate mentioned funds are obliged to return to Prozor municipality immediately. So this was a way how you requested from those abroad that were not paying any taxes into Prozor municipality, they either report and they are mobilised, or they pay 30 percent of their monthly salaries into Prozor funds. And then what I think is also important here, in Article 4 it says that payments of funds shall be done through Coordination Committee Rama with head office in Munich or in Prozor municipality for the war budget. Again, attempt by individual local municipalities to collect funds and to even have an office in Munich, this Coordination Community Rama to collect those funds. Certainly economically unviable measure, but a measure which was adopted out of the needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 02995. 1D 02995.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an early decision of April 7, 1992, passed by the assembly of the Ljubuski municipality on obligatory solidarity allocation for the needs of defence of Ljubuski municipality; and Article 2 is an example of what Your Honour has suggested before, and it says: "All persons employed in public and private companies and shops are obliged to allocate solidarity funds. The amount of allocation is 1.000 dinars." This is a kind of a new tax on top of their net salaries, a special solidarity fund. Now, what was 1.000 dinars at that time, I don't know, but most likely it was not a very big amount, but the assembly of Ljubuski have identified that, you know, 1.000 dinar is what people can pay. Then, of course, it says that those funds shall be done to the account of funds for joint needs for Defence of Ljubuski municipality - I'm reading Article 3 - and then the account number is here, when the first salary is being paid, which means that it is active as of now on, and here in principle, employer had been request to pay that for the employees. Was he for that very reason reducing net pay or he has just higher cost, I can't comment; I can't see that out of this document. But, again, it is a measure of additional new fiscal revenue to support the defence and to collect money for the social services of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we go on to another municipality now, and let's look at 1D 01771.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document of May 2nd, 1992, by Posusje, a decision on obligatory financing of defence. And here, it says, similar as we have seen before with another -- with - just a second - with Prozor municipality, the Posusje municipality in Roman ii decided that: "For the citizens from the territory of Posusje municipality who are permanently employed abroad, the obligation is introduced to pay monthly the amount of 200 Deutschemark or the value of that amount in another currency for the needs of financing of national defence of Posusje municipality." When I visited Bosnia-Herzegovina in December of 2007, I talked to people about these type of measures, and the notions that they were telling to me is that they were, of course, identifying such measures, and then more or less all of them, you know, tried to impose taxation on those that worked abroad. But again, a measure, individual measure, new tax undertaken by another local municipality, in this case, Posusje municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, again, staying with the same municipality, if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, excuse me if I interrupt. It seems to me that this is very repetitious. We have I don't know how many examples. They all go into the same direction. They illustrate the point I think quite markedly. I wonder whether it is really necessary to have such a huge amount of more of the same? You are not the one that does not complain of lack of time, and I wonder whether this is really the best possible use of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if I -- Your Honour, if you're making a finding of fact on this particular issue for which I can count on in the final judgement, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There is no charge on Ljubuski or other municipalities collecting money, so I don't see which point of the indictment alleges that as a crime. I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll spell it out with three simple letters: JCE. It goes to the JCE. This is the whole problem, Your Honours. I mean, I did not draft the indictment. I certainly did not go ahead and put the imprimatur of the ICTY on it, but I have to live with it. And we're trying to show that measures were taken everywhere; the same measures are going on all over the place. Why? Because the Prosecution is alleging that there is an attempt to Croatise; there's an attempt to create a state within a state. Here, we're showing that all these municipalities are doing the same thing under very difficult circumstances. They're taking reasonable and necessary measures. It goes against the JCE. That's all I'm trying to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. I understand that perfectly, and I think you have done a lot of it, and I do not see the added value of added examples because this is all -- as far as I can say, so far it's quite -- this point, I think you have really well made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I'll go to the next bullet point, and I'll try to get the other documents in by way of motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree with my fellow Judge. You have amply demonstrated with all these documents that a high number of municipalities were -- whatever they were, they were doing the same thing. We can see that. But just by way of curiosity, Witness, we see that all municipalities will tax the workers who are abroad. Here, for instance, we've seen 200 Deutschemarks. Now, let's imagine that in a Muslim municipality this text is implemented; but the dweller, the inhabitant living there who is working abroad, he is a Croat. That means that the Croat will pay 200 Deutschemarks for the needs of the Muslim municipality. Let's do the opposite now. We are in a Croatian municipality, that of Mr. Topic, say, and does the same, and he requests 200 Deutschemarks from the Muslims working in Munich. Did you address - in my view - not to determine whether there were remittances of monies coming from other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we have show yesterday and, I mean, the documents were -- there were these taxes also imposed in Jablanica and in Tuzla region. What I have none not seen in these documents, I have not seen that the -- Posusje, for example, requested that these war tax shall be paid only by the Croats or the other way around. I have not seen this. I mean, gastarbeiter is gastarbeiter with a permanent resident in a particular local community, and they were of a different nation, but they were all at that time Yugoslav citizens or Bosnia-Herzegovina citizens. So I have not seen any of the, quote, "differentiations" by the -- what is a nationality of particular -- everybody was trying to, you know, defend the house he owns in Posusje, and by, you know, paying this into it, if he could not, you know, be mobilised and go into it, that's what he contributed to so that his house he had built with, you know, his savings or in Tuzla for the same sake. So that's what they were doing. And yes, they were -- I mean, the local municipality have, you know, invented these taxes both because they were authorised to do it and because there were no other means from the central government to ensure defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you tell us more precisely until what time this system operated? Throughout until March 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way I see that is that throughout the Bosnia-Herzegovina, you have those measures practically up to the point that there were some other region-wide measures implemented, and from what I could see later on is that once the -- in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, region-wide taxation was imposed, and this slowly had been, you know, vanishing out. But in the case of, as we had seen yesterday, Zenica and Travnik and even Tuzla, because the situation in Tuzla, from what I understand to discussing then, was much more difficult in 1993, some of these taxes were imposed once in the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna were already given up. So the type of the measure was in place practically throughout the war, but in different areas in different times, and that's why it was so difficult for the executive authority once established to really go with region-wide measures because if a particular municipality was well off because they have a lot of gastarbeiter, they will say, No, this is our money; we don't want to share it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could skip the next three documents in your binder, and we'll just go to the next bullet point rather quickly, which deals with -- to allocate fiscal revenues into the budget. The next document, sir, is 1D 00561.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document by the Mostar municipality where it says in -- on -- it's the decision of June 5th, 1992, and it's a decision on the allocation of basic and special sales taxes on goods and services. And in Article 1, it says that: "All legal and physical entities and all legal and physical persons conducting business in Mostar municipality and liable for tax on sales of goods and services are obliged to calculate and pay the basic and special taxes to the giro account of the war budget of Mostar municipality." Which means that they have not just collect fiscal revenues, but they were allocating these revenues not for their own needs but into the war budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we can look on to the next document, which refers to as a way of an example to your bullet point to collect revenues for particular social services. The next document is 1D 02990.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document which tried to -- which, of course, proves what I, you know, put in the bullet, that they organised themselves for -- that they collect funds and -- or later, we'll talk about organisation, to collect revenues for particular social services. Here, what we see is a decision of August 21st, 1992, document 1D 02990, of the Ljubuski municipality where in Article 1 it is defined that the health centre Ljubuski is allowed to introduce participation payment for health services pursuant to proposed lease as follows, and then it says that 100 dinar shall be paid for the general practitioner check-up. Just for your information, such a measure was imposed in Slovenia only once we you know, undertake the reforms of the health sector in 1994, 1995; but here it's a measure to collect revenues to ensure that the healthcare centre shall continue to operate because the health care centre Ljubuski, which would have to be financed by the Self-Management Interest Community for health care from the level of the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was not receiving funds. People need to go to the general practitioner; they had to pay. What I think is important, that in Article 2 there are exemptions, who is not to pay this participation, which means that the economic situation of a particular individual is taken into account and, of course, it says the -- that the army member shall not be being paid, pregnant woman shall not paid these contributions, pregnant woman, children under 14 age, person with chronic diseases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And finally, the last bullet point, there's one example that you wanted to share with us, and that's 1D 00544 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas. Witness, on this last document, I have the following question for you: In terms of a possible discrimination, let me take the theoretical example of an inhabitant of this locality, Ljubuski, has a wife and two children. That individual is aged 24 years, and as he knows that he belongs to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he has decided to enroll in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and he's gone off, I don't know where, perhaps to Sarajevo or to some Territorial Defence unit because he wishes to defend his country, in particular because there's Serbian aggression. His wife and children still live in Ljubuski. He's gone off to do his military duty. If we apply this text in this situation, he will not be exempt because he is not -- doesn't belong to the HVO army. His neighbour, his neighbour who has joined the HVO is exempt, but he isn't. Isn't there a problem there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think that he would fall under the last category: persons of poor material status. It is known that the Army of BiH was not being paid, so he will not have funds. The same manner, his wife would, of course, most likely be under that term. So I don't see this situation. So he would -- I mean, there are six lines, HVO army members, pregnant woman, and then there's the last one, persons of poor material status. I also kind of, you know, was trying to see whether that would be the case, but, you know, given the last line, and he would certainly be of a poor material status because he -- from what I understand and looking to the war budget of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the wages were not really paid to the army members, and he was not employed; he would be mobilised; he would be of a poor material status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if he owned his house, he would have money because six months prior to that he was earning a good living in Germany and he has returned to Ljubuski and that, in fact, he has a Mercedes parked outside the house, his wife has a television, a fridge, and they have no difficulty whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, I could explain that even today in the, let's say, countries that transited from the former Yugoslavia, we only look into the incomes. We are not yet able to look into the - what you call it - the assets of a particular individual. So if he would show that he does not have income, nobody would say, Okay, you have to sell the house or you have to sell the Mercedes parked or the TV, and then, you know, you show up with this for the doctor. I mean, this is the situation which had had been -- one could say economically is not right, but this is the way the system works even today. In Slovenia, if you have a, you know, very low income, you are, of course, authorised to have the services and pay lower contributions. We don't look into the assets, real assets or net wealth of an individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not like the Registry of the ICTY, Your Honour, when determining the ability of an accused to make contributions. If we go on to the very last document, 1D 00544, which is to organise for particular social services, and there was one example, and we'll finish up with this slide.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is example where on May 21st, 1992, Mostar municipality issued the -- adopted the following conclusion, to proclaim the hospital in Mostar a war hospital. In that context, it says in Article 2 that all the capacities and activities of the hospital must be put in the service of liberation of the town, which means that they, of course, re-organise their ordinary programme of operation, et cetera, to support the activities of the liberation, which is, again, the way municipalities organise themselves to cover the social services.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could move on now to the next slide, and if we could move at a quicker pace so we could wrap it up as expeditiously as possible.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What was the result of these independent actions by local municipalities in the territory of the Croatian Community and also elsewhere? Well, clearly, local municipality only took care of their own economic area. But they could not -- or they were not interested in undertaking some of the measures that one would of course like to see that would help those local communities that were of a lower level of income generated. Especially, that became problematic as far as the infrastructure is concerned. If a breach was down, and that breach, of course, was a bridge important for not just one local municipality but for the other, as well, a particular local municipality in which maybe there was that bridge only took necessary care to make, you know, a path around it; but, of course, they were not concerned about undertaking region-wide repairs, telecommunications, local communities collecting taxes, either in cash, et cetera. They were not very much interested to support development of the infrastructure, telecommunications, by which their local Social Accounting Offices would start to need paying funds into the wider region budgets. So I'm also mentioning in the report that once in the fall of 1992, kids were about to return to schools. Situation in particular local communities were different. Some of local communities have sufficient funds to ensure, you know, teachers' pay, books, notebooks, et cetera, for the kids. Others were not. If you want to send students back to university, you need to collect funds at the region-wide level to re-open university of Mostar, and that's why for this very reason, in this first period, the Presidency of the HZ had been established as the coordinator between the local community, and the presidency have started to undertake some of the measures that would -- at the region-wide level, at the region-wide level to somehow provide good economic environment. And that's why I say that already in this first phase it was good that the presidency already adopt some of a decision like a decision on the public enterprises in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna where it says which are, and here I would like to refer to document 1D 02018.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct. Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where in Article 1, it says that interest -- in the interest of socio-economic developments and the protection of nature and the natural resources of the Croatian people and other peoples in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna has adopted a decree establishing public enterprises in the following areas: First one, A, production, transmission, and distribution of electrical energy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Slow down. Slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Slow down and enunciate.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Im' sorry. A, production, transmission, and distribution of electrical energy; B, water management activities; C, forestry activities; D, mining activities; E, postal, telephone, and telegraph services, et cetera, all those enterprises that have region-wide importance. I would like also to refer to Article 3 saying the public enterprise shall be managed by a managing board appointed by the Croatian defence council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, or the -- for the first time the Croatian Defence Council of the -- the Croatian Defence Council -- the Croatian Defence Council appearing, and it says that the presidency of the Croatian Defence Council in Article 4 shall appoints an acting director for the public enterprises, clearly measure that was positive and, of course, enable normalisation of the region-wide -- or the wide region than just one local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could -- I think we are ready to go on to the next slide, which would be slide 31, and for this we have two documents, and we have approximately 7 minutes before the break. Perhaps we could finish both the slide and the two documents. So -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this slide, we are still in the first phase, but already in the first phase it's positive that the presidency adopted decrees regarding reactivation and re-establishment of the Social Accounting Office, and here I would like to refer to Document 1D 0003 [sic]: "Decree on the establishment of public auditing service..." or a proper English translation would be Social Accounting Office, brackets, "... in the event of a state of war or imminent threat of war in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Article 1 establishes this office, and Article 3 gives an authority that a separate decree, which would be subsequently issued by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council shall prescribe more closely the internal organisation, powers, and tasks of the SDK, Social Accounting Office, of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, a measure important because if you want to implement the region-wide measures, you need accounting office. You needs tax administration. You need -- again, re-establishing cashless society, you need to ensure that there will be there government institution helping you in recreating economic environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To make sure that the record is correct and accurate, Your Honours, it's 1D 00003, so there's four zeros plus 3. I notice earlier it was three zeros. We have four zeros plus 3. Now, if we could go on to the next document. As I understand, it's 1D 00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this Document 00003 is interesting because there's a preamble that sets out the reasons why this decree is adopted, this aggression, the breakdown of the economy, suspension of legal transactions, the use of dinars, et cetera, et cetera. All is very well explained, and then the decree establishes or re-establishes the SDK, but from your standpoint - because you are a Defence witness, but given your Slovenian origin, you are neutral - if you had to deal with such a decree, would you have automatically mentioned the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, or would you have mentioned the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina but given the degradation of the state apparatus at local level it was necessary to establish this? So as a technical practitioner, how would you have drawn up this decree? But you don't have to answer. If you wish to answer, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no problem answering because I'm -- I try to be here as an expert. This measure should have been undertaken by Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It had not been undertaken. The Social Accounting Offices ceased to operate. Once the territory of Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna -- sorry, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna has been liberated, an authority had to reconnect those Social Accounting Offices. So in the way, the decree is of course written, especially the introduction where it says that, of course, that obviously other province in the Serbian Republic, the use of dinars of the federal republic, I think is the way to do it. It is to reconnect the economic area of not just one local community. If they would hereby establish the SDK for the whole Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that would be beyond their responsibility, right? This is the -- I understand issued by the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which is a group of local community. Perfectly, perfectly, given the presidency decree here, it would be -- says legally perfectly would be, while the district of Mostar as entitled to do that by the presidency decree of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on counties hereby issues and establishes Social Accounting Office of the district of Mostar. But I don't know whether they knew that at that time. But it is a logical reaction to go and create Social Accounting Office and even more, in the next document, 1D 00013, to establish customs administration on the territory. Why is this even more important document? Because with the establishment of customs administration, they establish a border between Republic of Croatia, and what used to be administrative border of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which now becomes, of course, a border of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina where the control checkpoints of the customs administration that has been established was up and running, all in order to normalise economic activity in the area of not just one local community, but many local communities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you've just said two important things in your answer, and as part of the cross-examination, the Prosecutor might return to these points, but it must be on record. You have just said that Mate Boban, who signed this document, was in fact acting as the head of a group of local communities. That's the first thing you said; and then, but this has been also mentioned with other witnesses, you have just said that the customs system that was set in place was tantamount to creating a border between the Republic of Croatia and Herzegovina, that is, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are two essential points. Are these the points that you highlight in your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both decrees are decrees on establishment of public auditing service and the customs administration in the event of a state of war or imminent threat of war on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I see this as a temporary measures, but they were the temporary measures undertaken in order to ensure economic-wide efficiency or region-wide efficiency. I never met Mate Boban. When I was reading these documents, these are very similar documents that one would undertake if you have or if you want, instead of connect and have a control over one local community, have economic control over bigger group of local communities. I have said earlier, Your Honours, reading the presidency of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina decree on districts - we will get to it - maybe it would be appropriate to put in the preamble, also, this decree, but then of course that decree puts local communities together in a different manner than it was done by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and that the way the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna local community were put together was really depending on what was the, you know -- what were the military activities took place. I would claim that once the customs administration was put in place, was put in place in order to prevent economic taking-over by Republic of Croatia, the territory of the local communities north of administrative border what was in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina because that's what they did. They established the customs, checking points so that they knew what is coming in and what is going out. If they were not acted, this would be economically very soon part of Dalmatia. Economically. This is what I'm saying. This is -- the analysis which I make is that these are logical economic measures one does in order to reconnect local communities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, you and I are looking at the clock. Did you have another document before finishing with this point, or can we have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think we can have our break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Sorry for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It would assist us in organising ourselves during the break to know how much time other Defence teams are planning for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. For the time being, Mr. Karnavas has used 3 hours, so in theory, he has another one hour. Maybe he won't need it. Based on the decision by the Trial Chamber, the other Defence teams will have two hours. I don't know how they split it up. Ms. Nozica, we haven't heard you in a long time. It was last year, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, and I'd like to take this opportunity to wish everybody in the courtroom a happy new year because this is the first time I've taken the floor. I remember what Judge Antonetti said, that this will be the best year for us, and before I begin my Defence case, I wish to believe that, and I wish to tell you straightaway that the Defence of Mr. Stojic has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What about you, for Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to consult with my client. There might be some, but we will be certain after this break. Mr. Praljak shall give me that he have some. I still don't know what exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on behalf of the Petkovic Defence, greetings to you all, and a happy new year to you. The Defence of General Petkovic has no questions for this witness because I think the witness was very clear and clear in his explanations and put all the relevant facts before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. On behalf of the Coric Defence, I would also like to wish everybody a happy new year. The Defence of Valentin Coric has no questions for this witness either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we didn't ask for any time for the cross-examination; and therefore, we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may be that Mr. Praljak and his counsel need some time, but they will see. So this is the situation now. Let's have a break, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of time, we are not really under pressure, under any time constraint, because the other Defence teams told us what they plan to do. I don't know what the Praljak Defence intend to do. They may say this straightaway. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I can tell you straightaway. We consulted and Mr. Praljak would like to ask the witness a few questions himself in view of the fact that he lived in the area at the time, and so he can throw light on certain interesting elements, particularly those having to do with the pre-war situation and the things that the witness himself talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, the fact that he lived there does not endow him with any particular expertise, as per the Trial Chamber's decision and confirmed by the Appeals Chamber. He needs to have some technical know-how. I don't think that -- I mean, I don't think that he has that many degrees. Among his many degrees, I don't think he has a degree in economics. I don't think that's the case. And with regard to taxation and everything the witness told us, I fail to see at all what would justify us sort of doing something else than what we decided before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Praljak has no specific knowledge about taxation or the monetary system or things like that. However, Mr. Praljak at the very least has the general education of an average citizen, and I think that is in keeping with the decision that you mentioned where the Appeals Chamber stated that at the very least where he has a special qualifications, then he can be allowed to do so; and as a citizen, he does have those qualifications as somebody who took part himself in the daily life of Croatia and later on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is why he does know about these problems and the kinds of problems that occurred and which the witness discussed here in one way or another. So the intention to highlight facts that happened at the time and in that area as an educated citizen who did indeed take an active part in economic affairs and events, he could see this and understand them as relevant events, and these are certainly the same events that the witness as an expert witness highlighted, too, so whether they had a direct link or an indirect link to the collapse of the country and the further economic development of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to discuss this with my fellow judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you noticed, we discussed the matter, and the Trial Chamber recalls that there was a decision, a very clear decision by the Appeals Chamber. To intervene, you must have some specific qualification. The Trial Chamber has always granted military qualifications or, in terms of electricity or gas or water, of public utilities to Mr. Praljak. But in economic matters, he doesn't seem to have any specific qualifications. If the Trial Chamber were to grant this, well, there would be no limit anymore. Mr. Praljak or somebody else could then speak to anything. So this is the position of the Appeals Chamber and also the majority position of the Trial Chamber. I'm the spokesperson for the Trial Chamber. Personally, you know what I feel. I don't have to say it again. So, Mr. Praljak, you are not allowed to ask questions. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect to the ruling since it was a majority ruling, I will respect it, but I have to say for the record, and if necessary we can come back to the matter tomorrow, the Appeals Chamber decision was not correctly interpreted. I haven't got it with me just now, but the decision was that the accused does have the right to examine, and then it said in particular when, and then after that the specificities were mentioned. So it said "in particular." He has the right to examine and in particular, et cetera, et cetera, when specific knowledge, circumstances, and so forth exist. So with your indulgence, think about your decision, and perhaps we can carry on with this discussion tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, if what you say about the Appeals Chamber decision is right, and I would be surprised, you are saying that Praljak is entitled to cross-examine, examine, and in particular in relation to this specific -- it would have a general right to cross-examine. That's not my reading of the Appeals Chamber decision. But we're going to have a new look at it. We're going to examine it again. But your interpretation I think goes way beyond what the majority of judges in this Trial Chamber said and was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Perhaps the interpretation wasn't correct or perhaps I didn't speak precisely enough. In your first decision before the appeal, the words "in particular" were used in the paragraph which explains the circumstances under which the accused Mr. Praljak would be allowed to cross-examine. So that's what you said, whereas the Appeals Chamber just pointed that out, indicated that, and I remember the sentence full well because I read it word by word, line by line, the decision of the Appeals Chamber and the ruling of this Chamber too. And I'm quite certain that after the decision made by the Appeals Chamber, the situation was cleared up. So your request, the request of this Tribunal -- this Chamber stands that he must have some specific knowledge, in particular when such and such is concerned. So this does not exclude other areas of knowledge. It doesn't call for specific knowledge that you said -- of the type you said military criteria and so on and so forth. It requires certain knowledge of the facts. Now, Praljak was there. That's a fact. He's an educated man. That's a fact. You've already heard that. He did have the power and capability of grasping certain developments in society including economic developments, and he was a subject of those developments as a citizen and partially as a businessman, so I do feel that he can ask relevant questions and that that is in keeping with the decision that you are referring to. And ultimately, you do have the instruments in your hands, and I don't think it would be proper to ban questions before they are posed. Any one of us, even well-trained Defence counsel or counsel in general, can put a bad question, by school definitions. It can be repetitive, leading, or whatever. You are there to correct that as the Chamber, and you did do so along the way. So I don't think it's fair to prohibit a question before it is posed. I've tried to be brief. I have just intimated the kinds of topics that he wishes to raise. If you would like, he will be happy to tell you of the basic areas that he wishes to discuss and cross-examine on, and he can explain why he wants to ask those questions. So that is just my comment. Your ruling stands. I can do nothing against that, but I wanted to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The Trial Chamber has decided to stop this discussion, not to give the floor to Mr. Praljak, but to ask Mr. Karnavas to proceed and continue. Let me just observe this, Mr. Kovacic. Mr. Praljak could easily have given you the questions he intended to ask during the break and you yourself could have asked the questions if indeed these were very essential questions for your Defence. That's all. That's what should have been done.
