He should have scribbled the questions on a piece of paper to say, You have to ask about this and this document, and you as a counsel, you could have said, Well, witness, as requested by Mr. Praljak, I'm asking you the following questions, and the matter would have been settled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that possible solution, Your Honour. I would just like to mention that Mr. Praljak yesterday, after this witness began his testimony or, rather, this morning, he read some literature and some material on the subject to remind himself of the substance of what he thought was relevant, and it will be rather difficult, but I think that we will be able to do some of that in the way in which you have suggested. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Praljak. I know you want to address the Judges and the Judges, my colleagues, don't want you to. What can I say? I am forced to comply with a majority decision of this Trial Chamber. That's all there is to it. I have told you that through or by writing down something, you could have asked your lawyer to put questions as part of the cross-examination on specific points for specific reasons because last night I noticed this and that and this document was interesting. And as your voice in this courtroom, the counsel could have said, Well, as requested by my client, I'm asking you, Witness, this or that question, or the counsel could also have said exactly what you wanted to ask. He could have read your questions and we would have avoided the problem. But my colleagues don't want you to take the floor. I can't go against a majority decision. So, alas, you have to sit down. Mr. Karnavas, please proceed. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: Does that mean that I'm not able to address the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you want to address the Court on another topic, I'm going to ask my fellow judges. But as to this particular item, that has been settled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Judges are telling you and that the accused has to express himself through his counsel. If you want to say that the detention conditions are unbearable, that you can say through your counsel. But personally, you are not allowed to speak. That's what my colleagues are telling you. But you are going to testify in a few weeks, in a few months' time, so keep your energy until then, until the testimony of which will be very relevant for you. If you deem that there are topics that you are not allowed to address now, you can deal with them when you testify, and then you will convey what is the truth for you. Please, Mr. Karnavas, with regard to time, you have one hour left. Based on our calculations, you had 95 hours, but the hour has been used, so possibly you might have 12 minutes for redirect. I wanted to tell you that. I have to be the gamekeeper. You know, we have to look into the situation, but let me tell you that once you have used up this hour, you will only have 12 minutes left because you will by then have exhausted your 95 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. President. Thank you for reminding us on that. For some reason, the time got lost. In any event, if I may be of some assistance regarding this particular issue between now and the time I finish, perhaps Mr. Praljak could write out the questions, and I'm sure that we'll take a break after I conclude, and during that break he can consult with his attorney because I'm sure that the Prosecution would like, perhaps, a break to set up before beginning the cross-examination, so an offer of proof on the record can be made. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think it would be best for you to finish with the examination-in-chief and then we'll have a break. Mr. Praljak can possibly talk with his attorney, pass some questions to him. That seems to be a very sensible idea. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, prior to the break, Mr. Cvikl, there was a question that came from the Bench based on one of the documents that we saw concerning the customs administration, and I thought that I would show you one particular document which is cited in your report on footnote 816. This is 1D 03004.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if I could get your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We will provide you with the document. It is cited in your report, footnote 816, and we have provided copies to everyone. This is just one additional document in addition to the ones that are -- have already been provided, and this is a decision on border-crossing with the Republic of Croatia, and I wanted to bring this to everyone's attention in light of the questions posed. If you could look at Article 2. And if you could -- do you recognise, first of all, those border crossings, more or less?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I recognise them as the border crossings on the what used to be administrative borders of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina before the -- before its independence and at that time socialist Republic of Croatia, so these are the, as far as I know, borders on the southern side of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And by looking at these border crossings, based on this decision, can you tell us with any degree of certainty whether these border crossings surround the area that was known back then as Herceg-Bosna, you know, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a map here, but if I'm not -- if I'm correct, these are the borders on the -- what I believe is the southern part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So in other words, it's between the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. So in other words, it's between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, if we can go back to your presentation now, and I believe we were about to start with slide 32, if I am not mistaken. If you could briefly look at the slide and give us a small commentary -- or short commentary, I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before we move on to slide 32, you said something earlier on that I found interesting and I mulled over during the break. Speaking about border or customs crossings and customs tax, you said that some kind of a border had then, thus, been created between the Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then you mentioned Dalmatia. I personally do not know Dalmatia. I do not know the beaches in Croatia, so I am really unaware of this topic. But I understood that with relation to Dalmatia, Croatia had the same sort of issues because of customs duties or the absence thereof, there seems to have been an absorption of Dalmatia into Croatia. Could you shed some light? It might be interesting, and since you offered this information, I suppose that you must have some reason for saying that. Could you expand on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Before I expand, let me just say one more important element with slide 31, and it has to do with basically both activation and re-establishment of the Social Accounting Office and of the customs office. I want to say this because I also read over the break again this preamble, not just of the Social Accounting Office recreation, preamble of the Document 1D 00003, but also the preamble of the Document 1D 0013 [sic], and the preamble of the document establishing the companies of customs administration in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna says starting from the fact that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has delegated the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness is kindly asked to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Has delegated the federal institution with its declaration of independence, and the fact that due to the state of war, it has not established a customs service in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and with the aim of protecting legal entities and natural persons in foreign transactions, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, pursuant to Article 8 and et cetera, issues the following -- issues the following decree: A document signed by then -- or the president of the HVO Croatian Defence Council, Dr. Jadranko Prlic. Why I mentioned earlier in my testimony the issue of Dalmatia, because Dalmatia is, you know, the southern part of Croatia, and I have said economically if there would be no borders, no customs, border crossing established as defined in the document 1D 03004, economically then Split as the biggest capital of Dalmatia would have economic influence also all the way to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and that's why I said that creation of borders and creations of the border crossings undertaken in the absence of activity by Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as defined in the preamble of the Document 1D 0013 has actually prevented that economically Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna would be integrated into area of Dalmatia, and with that, into the whole Republic of Croatia. Because no borders would mean that economically the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna would be dealing with, of course, enterprises in the area of Dalmatia, which is, we all know, Republic of Croatia. And that's why I have said that authorities in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna were in a difficult situation. Why? Local communities have undertaken measures, they could simply sit back and let Republic of Croatia enterprises and economic power which was at that time in area of Dalmatia, in Split, took over economically and economically integrate Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna local communities into, I said, of course, region of Dalmatia, but legally speaking, this is Republic of Croatia. And measures of creating Social Accounting Office and measures of the decision on border crossing and decision on establishment of the customs office during an imminent threat of war or a state of war and as said in the preamble because Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has not undertaken its measure were measured against integrating Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, economically speaking, into Republic of Croatia. I will give you another example from Slovenia. If you were not establish upon independence our border crossings on our southern border with Republic of Croatia, Istra, which is the most western part of -- peninsula of Croatia, would economically integrate western part of Slovenia into its own economic territory. So establishing of the border crossing in order to, as said, protect legal entities and national persons in foreign transactions is an activity which is economically appropriate activity if you want to connect local communities and for those local communities to remain within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me ask a couple of questions based on your answer, and, again, you were referring to, just to be precise, 1D 00013. From your own experience, when Slovenia became independent, did it establish a border crossing between Slovenia and Croatia, and did it do so by way of implementing some sort of legislation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We implemented this by the legislation. We have said that, of course, the federal legislation is not any more valued on the territory of Republic of Slovenia, and we imposed customs points, cross-checks on the very border, and also at the airport of Brnik which is, of course, international crossing checkpoints when you fly in Slovenia. And for that very reason, we were immediately attacked by the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was my next question. How long did you wait, weeks, months, years, to set up a border crossing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Declaration of Slovenia was announced in the parliament of Slovenia on the 25th of June. At midnight of that day, we established and we renamed Yugoslav customs officers into the Slovene customs officers, and we placed the Yugoslav flag and the title of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with the title -- with the signs Republic of Slovenia, customs point, and Republic of Slovenia border immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And now through your involvement in this particular case, having also travelled in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you come across any legislation signed by the president of the presidency Alija Izetbegovic at the time when Bosnia-Herzegovina was declared independent whereby he established border crossings in a customs administration?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not. I have seen only delegation of the federal law, but I haven't seen establishment of the customs administration of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I have not seen establishment of the customs crossing points by Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina I believe not all the way up to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Recognizing that you are here as an expert on economics, however, you've told us your background, and you've told us that you were involved during that transitional phase when Slovenia declared itself independent, based on the questions that were asked by the Trial Chamber, can you answer this particular question: Is that a particular activity that should have been carried out by the president of the presidency or the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina the moment Bosnia-Herzegovina declared itself to be independent?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it should be. That's what I have said. It was international-recognised state but did not take measures to become an effective state. It did not establish custom points at their external borders, at their former administrative borders of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one last question. Looking back at 1D 00013 where you mentioned that this document was signed by the president of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, of HZ HB, Dr. Jadranko Prlic, if we look at -- above the signature, do you see where it says Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it then says, starting from the fact that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has derogated the Federal institutions with the declaration of independence and the fact that due to the state of war it has not established a custom service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, but I want you to go back -- I want you to go to the last page, right above where we see Dr. Jadranko Prlic, and before we see the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna Croatian Defence Council, what do we see?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we see the whole title of the area, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you being from the region, in reading that, would you draw any conclusions as to whether the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is outside the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or within and subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This question is beyond the scope of the witness's expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's an invited response -- given that the Trial Chamber, which is entitled to ask questions even beyond the scope of direct examination and has indeed asked questions beyond the scope of direct examination, this is an invited question based on what came from the Bench; and therefore, having, again, if I may recall yesterday, there were -- and today there were questions concerning the gentleman giving opinions of a political nature, albeit he is here as an economist, I think this is well within.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This expert witness is an economist, but he's had a political function. He was a minister in his country for European affairs, so I suppose that he has some extended knowledge of quite a few points including political matters. Witness, can you answer or not? It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And my answer is as follows: Clearly, the legislation the way it was set both as interim legislation and, clearly, the way it was presented today me, it's a legislation that confirms to me that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was always within Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we can now turn our attention to slide 32, and if you could briefly comment on this slide, and as I understand it you wanted to draw our attention to a particular document, but first, if we could have a brief explanation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slide 32 explains what was the -- what is phase 2 of the economic developments. If in the first phase local communities provided logistic support, in the second phase of economic developments, in this area with -- known as Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Defence Council has been established, and I understand it as a temporary executive body. And in that context, now authorities, not just local communities, authorities, but also the regional authorities started to act; otherwise, hundreds of people, hundreds of thousands of citizens would simply leave Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Why I'm saying this, they would not leave from the local communities where there was good -- where there was good economic situation, but they would leave -- they would depart from those local communities of that Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna where the situation was not that good. And in that context, the task of the Croatian Defence Council, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, was to establish common regional-based financial and fiscal system, simply note to undertake measures at the level of the Croatian Community that would strengthen the economic area of those local communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could look at P 00128, and perhaps you wanted to comment or draw our attention to a particular portion of this document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to point in this Document P 00128, English translation first, to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but really, you always overstep the limits of the translation in a way that -- I'm sorry to ask both of you to stop because, for example, now, the question which was raised by Mr. Karnavas originally, the answer of our expert Mr. Cvikl was also added there. Now, they have corrected this question and answer. But, again, there are difficulties for the interpreters. Let me ask you to accept whatever they have asked you to do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Cvikl, we do need to pause because we're both speaking the same language, so go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to point to the page 34 of Document P 00128. And in the last paragraph before section F, there is a statement, and this is the economic report of that Croatian Defence Council. And the statement read: It should be stressed that with the establishment of a Chamber of commerce, Croatia Osiguranje, insurance company and Hrvatska banka, commercial bank, conditions have been created for reviving the economy on the territory of the community. And this is a proof of that they have worked on establishment of banking institutions. Second, they have not just been dealing with economic or banking sector; they were also dealing with social services. And on the same page, 34 of that same document, there is a statement, the last -- the second -- one of the last sentences in the paragraph on the bottom: "Some schools began classes on 7th of September and others depending on conditions. It was the same with schools in central Bosnia. We have no information about schools in the temporarily occupied areas." From here -- from that, I understood that authorities, region authorities, have taken care of ensuring that at beginning of the school year, which in the countries of the Balkans were always September 1st, school started classes. I would like also to raise your attention to the page 35, the second paragraph, at the bottom of that second paragraph, the last sentence read: "Efforts are being made in cooperation with municipal HVOs to repair schools and ensure working conditions." And last point. On page 32 of that document, they point to the problems, but the last sentence on the page 32, the first paragraph on the top read: "Nevertheless, a total revenue of each year 1.188 million was generated until 31st December, 1992, which has primarily been used as has been said for Defence purposes but also on reconstruction and the work of other institutions on the territory of the community." All these were for me proofs that in phase 2, the temporary executive authority of the HVO were making attempts to utilize government tools of collecting revenues to undertake government expenditures but expenditures that go across the whole territory, and especially what was important there, of course, to start the school year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Cvikl, we talked yesterday and to some extent today about the need for having banks because the SDK wasn't working, but here on page 34, it mentions insurance -- the establishment of an insurance company. Why is that necessary, for those of us who are not from the region and may not appreciate the need for an insurance company.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from my understanding, the reason why you need to have Croatia Osiguranje, insurance company, established on the territory is to undertake an insurance agreement with other countries' insurance organisations so that cars with plates from Bosnia-Herzegovina could get an insurance green card, international transactions, so when they came to the crossing points between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, the car were allowed to be driven into Republic of Croatia, Republic of Slovenia, where they went to collect goods that were to be imported in that territory. Without having insurance, you can't provide logistics for the supply of goods and services in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe we can move on to slide 33.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On slide 33, I continue with defining what of course were activity undertaken. We already talk about customs authority, tax administration. And then, of course, I say that there was quite difficult for the authorities to undertake because the challenge was to establish a sound financial and fiscal system. I have said in one of the earlier slides, they could opt that they would simply print the money, but that would mean that they would have a hyperinflation generated by themselves. Now, they have decided to raise taxes, to raise taxes to undertake revenue generation from the collection of taxes, not borrowing, from, you know, anyone. And furthermore, with the fiscal revenues generated, they covered government expenditures that the population need. And I'm also mentioning that why it was so important for the temporary executive authority of the HVO to undertake that is because there was a difference between local communities. If all local communities would be equally well off, then there would be no need eventually for the Croatian Defence Council to be active. But there were some of them that were not well off, and they had to do in that manner. And as we then comment on that very slide, the first results were already achieved in year 1992 by limited collection of the revenues and, of course, by undertaking first measure despite the fact that, you know, they did not have all measures yet fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I understand you want to draw our attention to two particular documents, the first one being 1D 03003. If could you look at it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again, please speak slowly or read slowly so that we don't have any problems with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Document 1D 03003 is the decision on the war budget of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the period from April to September 1992, Official Gazette, secret strictly confidential 021. And here it is important, and I would like to raise attention to you to page 3. The page 3 says under the 778, then there's a total revenues 1 plus 2, it says that the total revenues of the war budget are 41 billion dinars. However, out of 41 billion dinars, 40 billion dinars are being financed from funds, from loans from BH Navodna banka, National Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was by more than 98 percent financing the expenditures of the war budget. So the total expenses, which on the bottom line equal to the revenues, total expenses, 41 billion equal to the revenues were by 98 percent generated by printed cash. This was situation on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as undertaken, as controlled by the central government authorities. The problem or the second what I would like to raise in this issue is that on the expenditure side, I have not seen any meaningful, meaningful transfer of funds to the local communities or to districts. This is the period when the districts were already established, but I do not see any meaningful funds being transferred down to the district. I would -- only would like maybe to point to page -- to page 11. You have section 34 on the top, and there it says that the Banja Luka lower court should receive 6.439.000 dinars. There were only limited outlays -- outlies envisaged for lower -- in that case, lower courts, but I have not seen any meaningful expenditures to cover activities of local communities or provision of social services at the local level. And that's why I, of course, point to this document because this document, which is the war budget of the whole country, did not provide funds for the activities needed to be undertaken at the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could look at the next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I've been listening to you carefully, and I noted that you said that looking at the documents, you failed to find any trace of fund transferred from the central government to local communities. Allow me to wind back a little to the times of the former Yugoslavia. In terms of justice and judges that were working in Mostar in the former Yugoslavia, as far as you know -- or we could take an example of judges in Slovenia. That would be exactly the same. As far as you know, during the time of the former Yugoslavia, who paid the Judges working in Mostar? Were they paid by their federal republic or by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or were they paid by local communities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have -- when we discuss the constitution, we have presented that the republics were responsible to finance judges, the judicial system. That's why I have pointed to the item when there was a transfer for the Judges even to Banja Luka, Republika Srpska region. But what was missing, what is missing in the war budget, the way it was defined under the decree which we have seen, there should have been expenditures for the local municipalities or districts if for the society -- if the whole society should be, of course, benefitting from the central government authority. Central government authority financed these expenditures by borrowing from the central bank but have not undertaken expenditures on the other side. That's why somebody needed to act, and that was the lower-level authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you take the example of Banja Luka. I prefer to stay with Mostar. So in the former Yugoslavia, in theory, the Mostar-based judges were paid by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is what you're saying. When the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina became independent, I suppose that the republic must keep paying the Judges. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is so, and that's why in the war budget that has been envisaged. In the war budget, we also have a line for Mostar. Was it exactly actually paid? I don't know. I haven't seen actual expenditures. But what am I missing in the war budget, I'm missing expenditures for other needs of the local municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but as to the Judges working in Mostar, whether they be Croats, Serbs, or Muslims, if they no longer get their pay once they do have work and -- work decided by authority, and work of authority, for the pursuit of this work of authority because without judges -- justice you just have chaos, so who then has to pay for the Judges? Do the local communities have to pay them if the Sarajevo government no longer pays the Judges for various reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would assume that since the war budget provided a very limited amount for the budget, for the Judges, the needs of the judicial system was later covered by local authority, and we would have an example on the slide 34 where we see that the local authority -- actually, in the phase 2 or the temporary executive authority, the Croatian Defence Council has undertaken the repair of the high court and basic common court of Mostar, which would be in normal circumstances a responsibility of central government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your study, did you look at budgetary documents of the time of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to see whether in the -- as part of the preparation for the budgets there was the inclusion of these republican budgets, be it justice, police, or others, and that there was in that case and via the SDK in Mostar there were payments from the budget of Bosnia-Herzegovina towards the SDK of Mostar so that the SDK of Mostar could pay the Judges? Did you go and check that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't checked the actual payments. I checked the Official Gazette with this war budget, but I understood that the telecommunications were down and that the Social Accounting Office based in Sarajevo did not have connections with the Social Accounting Office in Mostar to pay the Judge. So I do not know how much of these expenditures which were envisaged in this budget had been really undertaken. However, if as reported by the report of the economic department and the justice department of the HVO as presented on slide 34 in my report, the repair of the high court and basic communal court in Mostar have been undertaken by them, means that they were not receiving funds to take care of their own repair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'll consider a theoretical case with you. You're Slovenian; you have responsibilities, so it will be easier for you to answer. Let's assume that at the time of the aggression of the GNA on Slovenia that in Slovenia the central government no longer exists, is -- no longer has the wherewithal to pay its judges and policeman, and that in a remote region from your capital, that is, there are policeman, judges, military personnel; no one is paid anymore, whereas they have wives, families, children, et cetera. What would have happened in Slovenia in order to avoid chaos? What would you have done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would most likely went with a very similar matters. If, let's say, the war in Slovenia would not be just for two weeks and during those two weeks' times we were able to utilize some of the strategic reserves that were actually allocated throughout Slovenia in, let's say, free territory of Maribor region, which is the eastern part of Slovenia, most likely very similar measures would be undertaken. I now can also say that attack on Slovenia, which, of course, was a short war, two-weeks' war, was actually at one point in time close to a situation where Ljubljana would be attacked, and in these very circumstances, two things would happen: Central government would leave Ljubljana to the, you know, reserve position, and most likely in Maribor or northern part, similar type of measures that we have seen envisaged under the decree on districts by the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the measures undertaken by the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna would be undertaken. That would be done most likely in Slovenia at some 8 units, because that's what kind of a number of the quote regions we have, but this is the way the things would continue. We would see very similar measures. Now, how and what kind of measures would that be depends on how difficult the military situation would be. But, yes, one would in war economy situation see similar measures on a particular area of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, still pursuing my hypothetical assumption, so if Ljubljana had been under siege of the GNA with the government blocked in Ljubljana with no contacts with Maribor and that that lasted longer, one week, two weeks, a month, six months at Maribor, what would have happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what would happened, they would following the, basically, military plans, undertaking their own mostly collection of fiscal revenues, and then they would be paying policeman, army people, hospital employee, teachers out of that proceeds in order, you know, to keep people of Maribor, if this would be a free territory, continue to live. They would do a very similar activity which we have seen first at the level of local communities and later at the level of group of local communities. And Maribor, of course, is a big city and a lot of, you know, local communities kind of, you know, surrounded there, so you would see them working together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a follow-up to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of course, yesterday, you did talk about the self-management mentality or culture that had existed, and I take it that that -- that self-management culture was in place in Slovenia as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It was same system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And going back to the one question concerning the judiciary. Yesterday, on slide 26 you referred to a document, 1D 02047. You will find that in the first binder. 1D 02047. And I'm sure you will recall, this is the decree law on the application of the law on the financing of general social needs, and you directed our attention to Article 2. And then, again, you directed our attention to Article 3. So when you find it...

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at Article 2, point 1 -- point 2, Article 2 begins with: The general social needs of the socio-political communities during an imminent threat of war and during a threat of war shall be... and under 2 we can see the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, public Prosecutor's Office and public attorney's office, courts and penal and correctional facilities, and so on. And then if we look at Article 3 that you pointed out where it says that based on Article 2 of this decree, the needs shall be financed from the budget during an imminent threat of war and during a state of war from the appropriate funds of socio-political communities as required. So when I listened to you answer before to His Honour, Presiding Judge Antonetti, it seems to me that this particular decree dovetails the answer that you have given. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Object to the leading question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question, but I'm sure that the gentleman is capable of answering without me leading the question -- leading him. Here is the document, you heard the answer, and I'm asking him to again refer to a document that was already in evidence that we have already discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To what extent, looking at this particular decree, and keeping in mind the answer that you provided to us earlier, specifically to the question posed by the presiding judge, Judge Antonetti, does this decree in any way assist you in your answer, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First, decree law defines -- the law on the application, the law on the financing of general social needs defined in Article 2, number 2, that the central government should finance judges. But it also says in point 4 that there shall be additional resources to municipality, and in point -- it says in point 8 that it should be also the financing of the work of public services and particularly of health and social welfare. In Article 3, it says that all that has to be composed in the war budget. The war budget, the way it was defined, and this is the Document 1D 03003, has revenues, has funds for judges, but it is missing additional resources to the local municipalities, monies for public services, in particular health and social welfare; and thus, local communities were not receiving funds as defined in the decree law. So in the absence of these funds not being there, local communities and later regional communities had to act. However, since this is a decree law on the application of the law of the financing of general social needs and it's a general law and it talks about that there shall be a war budget, the fact that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna executive authority have identified the war budget is perfectly logical. I'm not a lawyer, so I couldn't say its legitimate. But it's perfectly logical that they have undertaken because central government have not financed the needs. So they went ahead with creating additional resources and in the war budget of now wider region of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna provide for the expenditures that shall be covered during the war or the situation of the imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we look at the next document very briefly, and this is a document that we saw yesterday staying with the slide that we're on, and this document is 1D 02959. I believe you wanted to draw our attention again to this document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will draw attention to page 1 of 2 of that document where the IMF analysed in table 31, Bosnia-Herzegovina expenditure shares in the year 1994, 1995. And of course, the most interesting for us is 1994 because this is the last year which I was looking to it. And we have seen that in the third column -- in the second column where the Bosniak majority areas is presented, in the second line, wages and contributions, there are no funds undertaken in the Bosniak majority area budgets to cover wages and contributions. This is connected with this Bosnian -- or soldiers in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the other side, we see that in the Croat majority area, 11.2 percent of the total expenditures had been wages and contributions. And the social fund expenditures - this is the 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 line - we see that Croat majority area, percentage of the total expenditures was 18.2 percent while much lower expenditures at the level of the Bosnian majority area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. Whatever is on the screen certainly isn't table 31, so just so everyone knows. But table 31 has been provided to everyone with our documents.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 102 of that document, which is now on the screen. Page 102.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's move on. We can put this on the ELMO if anybody wants it. Otherwise, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on. It's now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Continue very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is now the table 31, percent of total expenditures, and present that under the second column, Bosnian majority area, no expenditures under the line registers and contributions. 11.2 percentage point of the total expenditures were wages and contribution expenditures on the Croat majority area, and under the social fund expenditure line, much level higher of level of expenditures as percent of total expenditures in Croat majority area, meaning that in the area of Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, with government expenditures all needs of the society including the social fund expenditure and payments of wages and contributions were undertaken for the government employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We can move on to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you don't mind, we'll stay on the previous table. Registrar, if we could return to the previous one because I have a question to ask. Yes, we have the previous table, and there's something that I failed to understand and I'm sure you will be able to enlighten us. In column 2, the Muslim majority area, we see that in the column of figures under the title "Other," 58.2 percent, whereas in the Croat area it's .8. Why this significant difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this -- I don't know. I can't comment, but I would assume that these are all goods and services, this all under goods and services, and there seems to be -- military expenditures includes only reported cash expenditures that were carried on the budgets, so there could be some other expenditures under that very column. But the issue which I wanted to raise is the social fund expenditures and the lack of the wages and contributions in that report shows that -- and we also have been observing that, that the government employees in the Bosniak majority area were not paid or they were paid in kind, not cash. And we also know from this discussion, then, and looking to this report that the social fund expenditures in the Bosnian majority area, especially the pensions, were extremely low, while in the Croat majority area the pensions were paid out something like 60 Deutschemark per month. So there were attempts in the both areas which were different, and I'm only claiming that in the attempts in the Croat majority area resulted into a more normal structure of the government expenditures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning military expenditures, we note that in the Muslim majority area we have 25.4, whereas in the Croat majority area, 55.8, so almost double; but in 1995, however, we see that there's a reduction of expenditures in the Croat majority area and, however, there is an increase in the Bosniak majority area. Do you have any factor to explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, these are the level of expenditures, so these are the percentage of total expenditure. There could be two explanation. One is that in 1995 there could be result of the fact that in the Croat majority area you have a bigger economic boom, so with existing soldiers costs, you have other -- you have more revenues being generated and so the expenditure could drop down. The second possible explanation is that in 1995 - this is already Dayton or post-Dayton - the need for military was lower, so the people had been demobilized. But I have not been really looking into what was happening in the military, so I can't comment. The only what is obvious from that picture and also from other information in this IMF report is that the economic activity on the territory the Croat majority area as envisaged by the revenues levels of that territory and the revenues levels in the budgets was much stronger. Practically the figure is twice the size -- that the revenues in the Croat majority areas were twice the size of the revenues in the Bosniak majority area, which had looked as a proof that there were the positive effects for the well-being of all society if, you know, with all these measures which I was describing. That is -- that was for me a positive explanation. Also, when we were coming into Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1994, 1995 from the south, we could see this, you know, vibrant economy in the area of -- around Mostar; not so vibrant economy or difficulties in the area of Sarajevo; quite vibrant in the economy in the area around Tuzla; and difficulties, economies difficulties in the area around Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Final question concerning the roads. It's very surprising looking at the figures. We have the impression that in fact no one is interested in the roads, that at the outset the Bosniak majority areas had given some importance. We had 5.6 percent. The Croats were doing nothing. There's nothing there. And in 1995, that the Muslims declined quite significantly because we are down to zero, and the Croats do a little something, 1.3, whereas we all know that roads can be economic vectors. How do you account for that, for the IMF?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would assume that since the road repair, and the road maintenance is somehow linked with the road repair - I mean, it's difficult to say what all it is - were a very strong share of the post-war reconstruction programme; and actually, the first bridges on the Neretva river, which were down, I believe 1992, were actually repaired out of the war bank loans and other international donor institution, and that only came up in 1996, 1997. So I don't know what is behind this road maintenance figures in the Bosnian majority area, but I guess the importance of the road construction really, you know, came out much later. That's all what I could comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Final question because we could spend hours here, but we need to move to essential. An interesting sector, education, we see that through the figures that the Croats really did focus on education, whereas the Muslims were doing less. Is there an explanation for that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there's explanation for that, and I have mentioned in my report that one of the critical moment or one of the most important moment when the society at large in the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna realised the value added, the importance of the Defence council was actually in September 1992 when schools were re-opened because of activity by the Croatian Defence Council of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, not just the elementary schools, but also from the report I could read that the university re-opened its classes, first in Neum and later, again, in Mostar. I do not know what was the situation in -- in different local communities in -- on the area where there were mostly Bosniaks, Muslims, but figures shows that, yes, Croat-majority area budgets had a major impetus for the, you know, education, and the first economic region-wide measures were linked with that. And when people saw that, and as you know - at least I could read it - there were a lot of fights internally between richer on poorer local communities, when you present the richer local communities that you are not taking the money which they were collecting just to spend it somewhere else but to put it into schools, I believe the authority and the authority of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna has with debt being built up, and that authority was, of course, needed later when also the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been established. I understood from discussion with my, you know, counterpart that actually I don't know how much of, you know, really, elementary schools and how -- whether the university operated in Sarajevo. I don't think it did. But University of Mostar did operate, and students went to these classes in Neum, and later, you know, they stayed home. I also said in my report that that will not be done. People from the region of Herceg-Bosna could simply depart to Croatia, to Slovenia, and elsewhere, and these would be empty economic area, which of course would be, for those that could not go, extremely difficult. So there was a value added in focusing on provision of the state and social services, education, health, social fund expenditures, pensions, mentioned here, that actually was needed, and this is exactly what we would do in Slovenia if the war would continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go on to slide 34 very briefly because we do need to get into the third phase. But on slide 34, if could you just give us a few remarks, and then as I understand it, you wanted to redraw our attention to P 00128.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This slide discusses really what were the -- some of the expenditures undertaken by the funds collected at the area of wider region of Herceg-Bosna; and you can see repair of government infrastructure, rehabilitation and equipment of office, support to the university, chamber of commerce, pedagogy institute, institutions of culture, water-supply, police department, and last item, the high court and basic communal court in Mostar. I'm saying this because two years later in early 1996, when the first World Bank money was spent, the first World Bank money spent in Bosnia-Herzegovina went for the repair of courts of Sarajevo. Courts in Mostar had been already repaired by activity of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Should we go to P 00128, or should we move on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document just confirms, you know, just actually list all this type of repairs that were undertaken, so we could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, I see -- I notice the time, and I believe this is a time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Let's break. After the break you'll have 30 minutes left, so we'll no doubt -- and I hope the examination of Prlic Defence -- today. 20-minute break. We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I begin, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we have a half-hour left, so we'll have to go through the remainder of your presentation, which I do believe is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Judge Trechsel, for slide 35, we have several documents. If we get to the point of saturation, I'm sure you will let me know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's to assist you in your time management.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, but a hint would be welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at now slide 35. If you could -- now we are into phase 3. If you could comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In slide 35, we present the phase 3, which really started with the establishment of institutions, mainly the decision of constitution of the House of Representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and then there were a follow-up, monetary policy and financial measures undertaken, all of them to strengthen economic system. Very important, Deutschemark had been put in, into -- also, into domestic payments, all linked with the fact that you wanted to really support economic developments, and there was also further development in the financial sector; insurance companies were, you know, strengthened to provide -- for the authorities to provide much better functioning of the economy. In that respect, I also would like, of course, to say that the budget policy and measures undertaken for the interim budget 1994, with the documents that I could see, assumptions and basic data for the 1994 budget revenues and expenditures, they confirm that they have undertaken everything what wider economic area need to do when preparing its budget and its expenditures. So the phase 3 is a phase where the economy was rounded, and thus, such Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was economically very easily to be integrated into the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina once this agreement had been reached. And again, these are measures that were expected given the war economy and expected given the fact that local communities' independent actions would be negative for economic developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can go through some of these documents that you have selected as examples. We can start with P 04589.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as of October 11, 1993, when the decision on the House of Representatives is been defined, and that --while here, I would like to point to Article 7, where it says that the house -- on the second page of that English translation, where it says in Article 7 that the house of representatives shall approve the republic's budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. If we go on to the next document, and again, I'm going to ask you to have a little pause and enunciate. P 09551.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is English translation of the document, which are the reports of the government and of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and on page 36, it explains under the Article -- under the title "payment system" that the payment system in Croatian dinar was realised to payment system office, which was established upon the transformation of SDK at the end of 1993, and then explains the -- which municipalities were included. Also it says in the last sentence, after founding the Hrvatska banka company Mostar and LT comerciana banka company Livno, the external payment system was established mostly with the Republic of Croatia. Then it says in the third-from-the-bottom paragraph: "As opposed to the first half of 1993, when only a limited number of legal persons carried out payments through the payment system organisations, in the second half, a large number of users had opened giro-accounts either in HRD or in Deutschemark, so at the end of 1993, there were over 1.300 active accounts." A sign of a vibrant economy. Then I would like to point to page 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's find it. Pause a little bit. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: 42 out of 83. On that page, there are really two important figures which I would like to point. Page 42, I don't see it yet on the screen. English translation is the page 42, so there is information about the budget revenue, and it says that 104 thousand million HRD are the tax revenues, 52 are revenues from credits, and 57 are donations. On the page 42 on the top, there it says that the total revenues are 217 thousand million Deutschemark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This would be on page 43?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be on page - sorry - 43 on the top. It says that 217.000 is the total revenues, but only one-quarter, one-quarter compared to 98 percent as we have seen in one of the previous slides is being financed by credits, and then we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. When you say 98 percent, you were drawing our attention to a previous testimony. What are you referring to because we need to have a very clear record.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 98 percent is the amount of the borrowings from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to finance the needs of the war budgets in 1992, and here we see it only one-quarter, which means more ability created out of the normalisation of the economic activity in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna been undertaken, and thus higher tax revenues and thus less needs for borrowing, quite normal or normalisation of the economic situation. And then we see on page 43 a list of budget expenditures as defined for different ministries, and of course I think it is important to say that practically all ministries are involved in the budget expenditures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we move on, when we look at this particular document, the way the budget is laid out in a rather transparent fashion, can you tell us to what extent this would mirror sort of the -- another budget, say, from the area, from that particular region?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have been deputy minister finance and secretary of the ministry of finance in the republic of Slovenia, and we were preparing before reforms in 1999 a very similar type of budgets. Of course, we are more lucky that we did not need to borrow more than maybe 5 percentage points, but, you know, this is because of the economic circumstances. But on the structure of the budget, the pre-conditions for calculation the needs, quite exact estimations of the number of people, wages, et cetera. This is a type of the budget that one could expect in the region before, of course, those reforms had to be undertaken as one entire European unit, but that was not expected in the 1994 period yet here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just one final question because I'm not -- I'm a little confused, perhaps. On page 42 where we looked at revenues from credit, 52, and then donations, we saw 57, and then you told us that a quarter, based on the total amount from page 43, you use that figure as opposed to 98 percent, the 98 percent being from Bosnia-Herzegovina, the republic, and are we to understand based on your testimony yesterday that that's the 98 percent where the central bank was just basically printing money with nothing to back that currency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly true. The 98 percent referred to the war budget of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina where the money had been printed by National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Here, I understand these are the revenues from credit mainly provided by commercial banks because we have not seen and I have not seen any central bank being created on the territory of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which means that, also, these revenues from credits had been backed by some savings in commercial banks, and I guess that were at that time mainly so-called Hrvatska banka Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And incidentally, that 98 percent that you indicated, was that from the document that we saw earlier concerning the war budget, which would have been 1D 03003?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document of the war budget of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we go on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One follow-up question. This document we have still on the screen about expenditures broken down by ministries, mainly, we can see that for the Ministry of Defence, it is -- it represents just about 80 percent of the budget. Is that a classical ratio in times of war, or is this something rather exceptional?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the budget expenditures for the distribution for the January 1993 to December 1993, and given the fact that this is the time of the war, I would say, yeah, it's quite logical the highest portion of expenditures will be with the war. And as we have seen later on -- before when represented 1994 and 1995 figures as presented of the IMF document, that portion then dropped down to below 40 percent. But 1993, this is war, period. So it's logical that this was that high level of expenditure. But from my economic point of view, what was more important, there are other ministries there, and that's a full-fledged -- I mean, that's kind of a -- all ministries that one would expect to cover, you know, government needs, especially, you know, customs, financial police, ministry of work and social services, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in a period of war -- we have 170 million here in this document. What kind of expenditures were there? Are they connected to purchase of weaponry or -- well, it may not be a classical budget by European standards. Well, you have operational cost and investment costs. It's difficult to see what is devoted to -- earmarked to investments or to operations. But I suppose that out of the 170 million, most of it is devoted to purchasing weapons, while paying the sole dues based on documents that we have had an opportunity to see, that is done by local budgets, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At that time - this is 1993 - the most of the Ministry of Defence expenditures would go to finance defence units as, I guess, developed at a level of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and I believe the most of it would go either for the wages, for the outlays of the soldiers, and for the ammunition, weaponry, and all that. But I have no -- I did not have any detailed information into it. For me, reading these documents was extremely important that as we present what other departments were doing, and here I would like to refer to page 45 where you have description of the department for economy, and in the bottom of that there's a paragraph that there was the coordination and monitoring of the operation of public enterprises has continued, which means that they were making efforts to normalise economy situation. And this is why I have said that this is a normal structure of the budget. It is not just the, you know, war budget, military budget. This is the budget where government, where authorities have undertaken necessary activities linked with support of the whole economy. We have later on this case what they were doing in the forestry, mining industry, water resource management. These are all typical government activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Sorry. Thank you very much. I would like also to have a follow-up question or questions concerning the question which you raised, that is the lacking of support by private banks, which were in a way used by the central budget of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you mentioned the example, one of the -- one of the banks of the Hrvatska banka in Mostar. Now, my question is for if the Hrvatska banka was -- in Mostar, of course, belonged to the whole chain of banks, private banks that within Hrvatska banka system, I believe which was a bank, private bank in Croatia, is my first question; or Hrvatska banka was a bank which had its headquarters not only in Zagreb but elsewhere. That is the first question. The second question is that if you have any more details concerning the composition of that kind of loan provided by Hrvatska banka to the central budget, if it was an important part of the budget as far as percentage goes or it was in a way negligible. And my number three question would be if you have any details or any data as far as those people, either private people or firms which contributed to Hrvatska banka, I mean by depositing money. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for your question. As far as Hrvatska banka joint stock company Mostar is concerned, in my document I also refer to the fact that this is a bank which was licensed by National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, I believe, and it was composed of what used to be branches of Croatian banks that had their headquarters in Zagreb. They had a branch in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but in 1992, this bank was re-established so the branches had to ask National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina for a licence to operate on the territory as an independent legal entity. By accident or by the fact that in 1997, 1998 period I actually worked in Nova Ljubljanska banka, which is one of the banks in Slovenia, and we at that time visited Hrvatska banka Mostar joint stock company, and we saw its ownership; it was owned by -- it was a Bosnian bank. We actually -- the Slovenia bank were even considering wanting to buy that bank, but it was a bank which was relicensed. It was to a certain extent very odd why they did it in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and why the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina did it. But it was logical, logical legal act, because Bosnia and Herzegovina had become a new state, and a new state has to licence a banking institutions. So it was very legally appropriately that owners of Hrvatska banka, which were previous branches, ask the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina for relicensing, and they got a licence. Now, the depositors in this very bank were, from my understanding, mainly those holders of - I mentioned before the figure - 1.300 accounts, which were the private and legal entities, small shops, small traders, but also, I've seen that in 1995 and seen 1997 also some -- or the re-activated manufacturing enterprises. They were those that were actually holding -- you know, they were doing business with that bank and they were doing the deposits. On the financing, I did not have much details of the -- who actually provided sources of financing to the budget, but since there were no central bank on the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the only two other options, and that is that financing is provided by the financial system which existed then, and that is Hrvatska banka, Ljuna [phoen] bank, insurance companies, et cetera. That is all what I can say on the base of the recommendation which I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have, first of all, a follow-up question or a question regarding your answer. You said first a few minutes ago that the Hrvatska banka Mostar was relicensed by Bosnia-Herzegovina, and later on - and this is on the last line of page 83 and then 84 - I read: It was to a certain extent very odd why they did it in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And you have also said that it was normal when there was a new state, new licensing was required. Can you tell us more about this relicensing by HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the relicensing was done by National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But it was done in the period when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna already exist, and I would like here to make a comment, which is like follows: If authorities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna would do nothing and they would not relicense or request that the branch of a bank based in Zagreb request a licence from Sarajevo, National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in a much quicker manner, economically, territory of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna would be economically part of Republic of Croatia. And why I say odd? There -- of course, these banks in the pre-war time could operate throughout Yugoslavia. Now, with the war they could not continue to do that unless there would be an agreement reached between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia that banks licensed in a particular country could operate across borders. Such agreement was not reached, so it was logical that they have requested for relicensing. And relicensing went against the economic interest of Republic of Croatia, so the owners of those branches, you know, had to do another effort. And of course, by getting a licence from the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this now became Hrvatska banka joint stock company based in Mostar, and it could operate only on the territory of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I believe later on it was quite successful bank, and I believe it's now owned by UniCredit in Tesa, one of the Italian big banks. We looked into that bank in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. The other question was, what we have looked at as "budget," I take it that this is a very condensed excerpt just taking the sums per ministries whereas the actual budget, which was elaborated, would have been much more detailed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The actual budget, if you want a more detailed information of the budget would in principally be much more detailed, and I'm sure that one would look to a particular section, could get much wider information, but this is what I got. I did not have any more information, and even that, when I was reading -- especially when I was reading the Croatian versions of that and, you know, B/C/S versions, I could see that this is, of course, a different approach, more economically sensible, and the budget reflects the overall positive economic developments in the territory of Croatian Community and later Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I had also understood it this way, and of course I do not think the Chamber needs, actually, more detail. I was just making sure. Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a follow-up question to the questions concerning the bank, and I'm going to be asking a couple of leading questions, but I'm sure I'll be stopped if I get too far ahead of myself. In the course of your examination in trying to prepare your report, you came across documents that, as I understand, and we have seen here in court from the central banker at the time from Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Andrit [phoen]. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it's based on those documents that you answered the questions posed to you by His Honour?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, we're going to skip some documents so we can finish on time, and I'm going to direct your attention now to P 07628, so we'll skip two documents in your binder and go to P 07628. This is another interim budget. If you could look at that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if you could kindly comment very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document, interim budget of the republic from 1994, and on page 1 of that document, first there are basic principles of the budget. I'm, you know, somebody who is dealing with the public expenditures management issue, and just the first line reading: The budget is balanced on the basis of gross principles. This is a very logical, normal, but extremely high standard of preparing the budget, which means that all revenues and all expenditures are to be presented. Second line, it says that: "Legal regulations on taxes and duties pertain to all state organs, municipalities..." et cetera, is explicitly envisaged in the legal regulation. Again, a good sign of a good public expenditure management. Last line on that page 1: For all procurement, a tax on the sale of products, et cetera, is to be paid, which means, again, no exemptions from government expenditures as far as the paying of the taxes is concerned. And I would like to refer to page 2, line - 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 - 5: The ministries and offices which needs to procure materials, fuels, lubricants, equipment, and other needs exceeding 100 Deutschemark per year are obliged to organise a unified procurement financial accounting service, a good practice requesting good public procurement in order to prevent fraud, negative effect, et cetera. So all these principles that one would like to really see put in place in all countries of transitions, which was of course not the case. I would also like to refer, if I may, given the time constraint, on page 4. There is chapter 2, data for the assessment of revenues and spending. And there's some figures, population, employee, et cetera. What is important, these figures are what usually one does when start preparing the budget. So a very clear instructions and very clear information given to whom? Most likely to the parliament of the house of representative of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna on how the budget had been prepared and had been adopted, which means these were for me all clear signs that you can assess that the 1994 interim budget expenditures, interim budget reviews are of a very similar type and extent as in normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go on now to the next document, P 08035. This is, again, another budget.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. If we have seen before the interim budget, which is usually prepared when the real budget is not prepared, here is the document P 08035, which is the budget for the six months of 1994, already approved, and it follows the same very good principle. The only difference that the English translation does not have on page 1 and page 2 appropriate figures. But an important information which I would like to present to the Chamber is that before the basic principle for the budget, there are two lines on top of it, average salary and average pension. And in the Croatian translation, that is presented as average salary 150 Deutschemark and average pension of 60 Deutschemark. This is 1994. This is a very good result for the post-war situation. Again, for me, a sign that by 1994 in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, economic situation had almost normalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we're going to skip the other documents that relate to this slide, and those would be 1D 00028, 1D 00026, 1D 0019, and we already skipped 1D 00032 and 1D 00038. But as I understand it, these were the sort of documents that you had selected in order to support your presentation here today, which, again, these are just examples?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. This examples presenting what kind of measures could be undertaken to put together the budget that we just presented, both on the revenues and expenditures side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. With that, let's go to the very last document that you have, and that would be for slide number 36.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The slide 36 talks about realisation by authorities, both the presidency of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as the regional authorities, that there is a need to establish mechanisms for coordination between local communities. And the document 1D 00509, issued by the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on August 13th, 1992, and the document is decree with a power of law on establishment and work of district, was for me a recognition by the presidency that if in a country with around 4 million people, 100-plus small ministates were to be -- were to create, the central authority had to found an intermediate solution, and that is establishing seven districts. Now, the document read, and I have and analysed it extensively in my document, what this decree -- what these districts have to do. And these districts, especially as defined in -- on page 3 where there is chapter Roman iii, rights and duties of the districts, and then it goes Article 8, 9, et cetera, it explains that actually these responsibilities of the districts are now from the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina vested authority down to the district that would be normally a state function. I would like to refer, also, to chapter -- to page -- to page, just as an example, 10, Article 40. In this Article 40, the presidency of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina said, that there will be seven districts, and there will be seven District Secretariat of Economy, and Article 40 reads: "The District Secretariat of Economy shall perform tasks and assignments namely..." and then it goes, in the field of energy supply, mining, and industry, undertake and propose appropriate measures for monitoring of accomplishment of production, et cetera. Then it explain what will be the field of agriculture, et cetera. These are classical functions of the ministries in any country.
